source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 6 (PDF 117-143, printed 117-143); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 6 (Chemical Energetics), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The study of the quantity of heat energy absorbed or evolved during physical or chemical changes is called:
blocks.explanation: Thermochemistry (also called energetics) studies the heat absorbed or evolved in physical or chemical changes (6.1).

book_ref.quote: Thermochemistry is the study of the quantity of heat energy absorbed or evolved

blocks.prompt: 2 Thermochemistry is largely based on:
blocks.explanation: Energetics is largely based on the first law of thermodynamics; Hess's law is a special case of it (6.1).

book_ref.quote: is largely based on the first law of thermodynamics

blocks.prompt: 3 The energy possessed by a substance due to its structure (types of bonds) and physical state is called its:
blocks.explanation: Heat content or enthalpy, H, is the energy a substance has due to its structure and physical state (6.1).

book_ref.quote: due to its structure (types of bonds) and physical state is called its heat content or enthalpy

blocks.prompt: 4 If the heat content of the products is 120 kJ and that of the reactants is 250 kJ, ΔH for the reaction is:
blocks.explanation: ΔH = HP – HR = 120 – 250 = –130 kJ; HP < HR, so the reaction is exothermic (6.1).

book_ref.quote: the total enthalpy of products (HP) is never equal to that of reactants (HR)

blocks.prompt: 5 When HP < HR for a reaction, ΔH carries:

options.text: a positive sign and heat is absorbed
a negative sign and heat is absorbed
a negative sign and heat is evolved

blocks.explanation: HP < HR means a lowering of enthalpy; heat is evolved and ΔH is negative (6.1).

book_ref.quote: HP < HR: such reactions involve a lowering of enthalpy

blocks.prompt: 6 A chemical reaction or a physical change in which heat is evolved from the system to the surroundings is called:
blocks.explanation: Heat evolved from the system to the surroundings defines an exothermic process (6.1).

book_ref.quote: in which heat is evolved from the system to surroundings is called exothermic process

blocks.prompt: 7 In an endothermic reaction:

options.text: HP > HR and ΔH is positive
HP < HR and ΔH is negative
HP > HR and ΔH is negative
HP = HR and ΔH is zero

blocks.explanation: In an endothermic reaction enthalpy increases (HP > HR), heat is absorbed and ΔH carries a positive sign (6.1).

book_ref.quote: HP > HR: such reactions involve an increase in enthalpy

blocks.prompt: 8 Which of the following is an exothermic reaction given in the chapter?
blocks.explanation: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = –393.7 kJ mol⁻¹, is exothermic; the others absorb heat (6.1).

book_ref.quote: For example, combustion of carbon in oxygen is an exothermic reaction.

blocks.prompt: 9 Cold packs used to treat internal injuries work because the dissolution of NH₄Cl in water is:

options.text: endothermic, absorbing energy from the surroundings

blocks.explanation: Mixing NH₄Cl with water absorbs energy (ΔH = +16.2 kJ mol⁻¹), producing a cooling sensation (6.1).

book_ref.quote: This reaction is used in cold packs (or ice packs) to treat internal injuries.

blocks.prompt: 10 According to the energy profile idea, in all chemical reactions:

options.text: bonds in reactants break before new bonds form
new bonds form before old bonds break

blocks.explanation: Reactant bonds must break before new bonds form, which needs collisions with enough energy (6.2).

book_ref.quote: All chemical reactions involve the breaking of bonds in the reactant molecules before the formation of new bonds.

blocks.prompt: 11 The minimum amount of energy required by reactant molecules just to cross the energy barrier is called:
blocks.explanation: Ea is the minimum energy to cross the energy barrier (6.2).

book_ref.quote: This minimum amount of energy required by the reactant molecules just to cross that energy barrier

blocks.prompt: 12 Bonds in reactant molecules can be broken only if the molecules:

options.text: collide with a sufficient amount of energy

blocks.explanation: Breaking bonds is possible only if reactant molecules collide with enough energy to overcome the barrier (6.2).

book_ref.quote: This can be achieved only if the reactant molecules collide with sufficient amount of energy

blocks.prompt: 13 The standard conditions for measuring standard enthalpy changes are:
blocks.explanation: Standard conditions: 25 °C (298 K) and 1 atm (101 kPa) (6.3).

book_ref.quote: Temperature: 25 °C or 298 K

blocks.prompt: 14 The standard state of carbon is:
blocks.explanation: The standard state is the most stable form at 298 K and 1 atm; for C it is graphite, not diamond (6.3).

book_ref.quote: the standard state of C is graphite not diamond

blocks.prompt: 15 The standard enthalpy change of formation of O₂(g) is:
blocks.explanation: By definition ΔH°f of any element in its standard state is zero (6.3).

book_ref.quote: the standard enthalpy change of formation of any element in its standard state is zero

blocks.prompt: 16 Enthalpy changes must be compared under standard conditions because the enthalpy of a substance depends on:
blocks.explanation: Enthalpy depends on physical state, pressure and temperature, so these are fixed as standard conditions (6.3).

book_ref.quote: The enthalpy of a substance not only depends upon its physical state but also on the pressure and temperature.

blocks.prompt: 17 The standard enthalpy of reaction is the enthalpy change when:

options.text: one mole of a compound is formed from its elements
one mole of a substance burns in excess oxygen
one mole of water is formed from an acid and an alkali
stoichiometric amounts of reactants in their standard states react completely under standard conditions

blocks.explanation: This is the definition of standard enthalpy of reaction; the others define formation, combustion and neutralization (6.3.1).

book_ref.quote: stoichiometric amounts of reactants in their standard states react together completely

blocks.prompt: 18 The standard enthalpy change of combustion refers to:

options.text: one gram of a substance burnt in air
one mole of a substance completely burnt in excess of oxygen
one mole of CO₂ formed from its elements

blocks.explanation: ΔH°c is for one mole of substance burnt completely in excess oxygen under standard conditions (6.3.2).

book_ref.quote: completely burnt in excess of oxygen, under standard conditions

blocks.prompt: 19 The standard enthalpy change of combustion of a substance is:
blocks.explanation: Combustion always releases heat, e.g. ΔH°c of ethanol = –1368 kJ mol⁻¹ (6.3.2).

book_ref.quote: It is always exothermic. For example, standard enthalpy of combustion

blocks.prompt: 20 Enthalpy change of combustion is especially useful for calculating:

options.text: the calorie content of foods and fuels

blocks.explanation: ΔH°c is used to calculate the calorie content of foods and fuels (6.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Enthalpy change of combustion is useful in calculating calorie content of foods and fuels.

blocks.prompt: 21 Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of methane?
blocks.explanation: Formation: one mole of compound from its elements in standard states: C(s) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g), ΔH°f = –74.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (6.3.3).

book_ref.quote: one mole of the compound is formed from its elements under standard conditions

blocks.prompt: 22 The standard enthalpy change of formation of a compound:
blocks.explanation: ΔH°f can have either sign; e.g. CH₄ –74.8 kJ mol⁻¹, C₂H₄ +52.2 kJ mol⁻¹ (6.3.3, 6.8).

book_ref.quote: It can be exothermic or endothermic. For instance

blocks.prompt: 23 The H–H bond energy is +436 kJ mol⁻¹. The standard enthalpy change of atomization of hydrogen is:
blocks.explanation: Atomization forms one mole of gaseous atoms: ½H₂(g) → H(g), so ΔH°at = 436/2 = +218 kJ mol⁻¹ (6.3.4).

book_ref.quote: when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element, under standard conditions

blocks.prompt: 24 Using the Cl–Cl bond energy of 243 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 6.1), the standard enthalpy change of atomization of chlorine is:
blocks.explanation: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g) forms one mole of gaseous atoms: 243/2 = +121.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (6.3.4).

book_ref.quote: The standard enthalpy change of atomization of an element is the enthalpy change involved

blocks.prompt: 25 The standard enthalpy change of neutralization is defined for the formation of:
blocks.explanation: Neutralization: enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by an acid and an alkali (6.3.5).

book_ref.quote: when one mole of water is formed by the reaction of an acid with an alkali under standard conditions

blocks.prompt: 26 For all strong acid–strong base reactions, ΔH°n is always near:
blocks.explanation: The only change is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), so ΔH°n is always near –57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ (6.3.5).

book_ref.quote: For all strong acid-base reactions ΔH°n is always near -57.1 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 27 When NaOH(aq) and HCl(aq) are mixed, the only change that occurs is:

options.text: formation of water from H⁺ and OH⁻ ions
breaking of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions into atoms
formation of H₂ and Cl₂ gases

blocks.explanation: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ stay as free ions; only H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) occurs (6.3.5).

book_ref.quote: the only change that occurs is the formation of water molecules leaving Na⁺ and Cl⁻ as free ions in solution

blocks.prompt: 28 How much heat is evolved when 0.25 mol of water is formed by neutralizing NaOH with HCl (ΔH°n = –57.1 kJ mol⁻¹)?
blocks.explanation: Heat = 0.25 mol × 57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ = 14.3 kJ evolved (6.3.5).

book_ref.quote: It is always exothermic. For example, the enthalpy of neutralization of NaOH by HCl

blocks.prompt: 29 The first electron affinity is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of:

options.text: gaseous atoms to form gaseous uni-negative ions

blocks.explanation: First EA: 1 mol e⁻ added to 1 mol gaseous atoms giving 1 mol gaseous uni-negative ions (6.3.6).

book_ref.quote: when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous uni-negative ions

blocks.prompt: 30 The first electron affinity of chlorine is –348.8 kJ mol⁻¹. The negative sign shows that:

options.text: energy is absorbed when Cl(g) gains an electron
energy is released when Cl(g) gains an electron
the value is measured in solution

blocks.explanation: Energy is released, so the first electron affinity carries a negative sign (6.3.6).

book_ref.quote: Since, energy is released, so first electron affinity carries negative sign.

blocks.text: 6.4 Bond energy (bond dissociation energy) and enthalpy changes

blocks.prompt: 31 Bond dissociation energy is the average amount of energy required to:

options.text: break one mole of a particular bond in a substance
form one mole of a compound from its elements
remove one mole of electrons from atoms
melt one mole of a solid

blocks.explanation: Bond dissociation energy: average energy to break one mole of a particular bond in a substance (6.4).

book_ref.quote: The average amount of energy required to break (dissociate) one mole of a particular bond in a substance.

blocks.prompt: 32 When a bond is formed between two atoms:
blocks.explanation: Bond formation releases energy; the same amount is absorbed when the bond is broken (6.4).

book_ref.quote: When a bond is formed between two atoms, energy is released.

blocks.prompt: 33 The energy of a particular bond in a particular substance (e.g. the C–C bond in ethane, 376 kJ mol⁻¹) is called:
blocks.explanation: A bond energy in a particular substance is the exact bond energy; the mean over many molecules is the average bond energy (6.4).

book_ref.quote: If we are determining bond energy of a particular bond in a particular substance, we call this exact bond energy.

blocks.prompt: 34 The C–C bond energies in ethane, propane and butane are 376, 356 and 352 kJ mol⁻¹. This shows that:

options.text: all C–C bonds have exactly the same energy
bond energy increases with chain length
bond energy is affected by the other atoms in a molecule

blocks.explanation: Bonds between the same pair of atoms have different B.E. values in different compounds because other atoms affect them (6.4).

book_ref.quote: For example, C–C bonds usually have B.E. values of approximately 350 to 380 kJ/mol.

blocks.prompt: 35 In practical calculations of ΔH from bond energies, we use:
blocks.explanation: Practically, average bond energies (Table 6.1) are used instead of exact ones (6.4).

book_ref.quote: Practically, average bond energy is used instead of exact bond energies.

blocks.prompt: 36 According to Table 6.1, which bond has the highest average bond energy?
blocks.explanation: Table 6.1 gives N≡N = 945 kJ mol⁻¹, higher than C≡C 812, O=O 498 and H–H 436 kJ mol⁻¹ (6.4).

book_ref.quote: Table 6.1. Average Bond Energies of Some Important Bonds (kJ mol⁻¹)

blocks.text: 6.5 Enthalpy change of reaction and chemical bonds

blocks.prompt: 37 A chemical reaction is a process during which:

options.text: old bonds are broken and new bonds are formed

blocks.explanation: A chemical reaction breaks old bonds and forms new ones; ΔHr comes from this (6.5).

book_ref.quote: A chemical reaction is defined as a process during which old bonds are broken and new bonds are formed.

blocks.prompt: 38 Which statement about bond breaking and bond formation is correct?

options.text: Bond breaking releases energy; bond formation absorbs energy
Bond breaking absorbs energy; bond formation releases energy

blocks.explanation: Bond breaking: ΔH = +ve; bond formation: ΔH = –ve; their difference decides the overall sign (6.5).

book_ref.quote: Bond breaking absorbs energy (ΔH = +ve) while bond formation releases it (ΔH = –ve)

blocks.prompt: 39 A reaction is exothermic when:

options.text: energy absorbed in breaking bonds is greater than energy released
energy released in making new bonds is greater than energy absorbed in breaking bonds

blocks.explanation: If bond-making releases more energy than bond-breaking absorbs, the reaction is exothermic (6.5).

book_ref.quote: Overall reaction is exothermic if the energy released in making of new bonds is greater

blocks.prompt: 40 The formation of water from H₂ and O₂ is exothermic because:

options.text: no energy is needed to break H–H and O=O bonds
H–O bonds absorb energy when formed
more energy is released in forming H–O bonds than is absorbed in breaking H–H and O=O bonds

blocks.explanation: Energy released forming H–O bonds exceeds that absorbed in breaking H–H and O=O bonds (6.5).

book_ref.quote: the net reaction is exothermic because more energy is released in forming the H–O bonds

blocks.prompt: 41 Using EH–H = 436, EO=O = 498 and EH–O = 463 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 6.1), ΔH for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g) is:

book_ref.quote: EH–H = 436 kJ mol⁻¹ ; EO=O = 495 kJ mol⁻¹ and EH–O = 463 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.text: 6.6 Measurement of the enthalpy change of a reaction

blocks.prompt: 42 The amount of heat evolved or absorbed during a physical or chemical change is measured by a:
blocks.explanation: A calorimeter measures the change in temperature to find the heat evolved or absorbed (6.6).

book_ref.quote: can be measured by an instrument called calorimeter

blocks.prompt: 43 At its simplest, a calorimeter consists of:

options.text: a burette, a pipette and a flask
a battery, electrodes and a voltmeter
an insulated vessel, a stirrer and a thermometer
a gas jar, a stopcock and a vacuum pump

blocks.explanation: A simple calorimeter is an insulated vessel with a stirrer and a thermometer (6.6).

book_ref.quote: At its simplest, a calorimeter consists of an insulated vessel, a stirrer and a thermometer.

blocks.prompt: 44 The specific heat capacity of water is:
blocks.explanation: It takes 4.18 J to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C, so c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (= 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) (6.6).

book_ref.quote: it takes 4.18J of energy to increase temperature of 1g of the water by 1°C

blocks.prompt: 45 How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 250 g of water by 12 °C (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)?

book_ref.quote: The energy is transferred as heat and is shown by relationship

blocks.prompt: 46 A glass calorimeter is NOT suitable for:
blocks.explanation: Gases would escape from the vessel, and products reaching high temperatures are also unsuitable (6.6.1).

book_ref.quote: However, it cannot be used for reactions involving gases which would escape from the vessel

blocks.prompt: 47 The outside walls of a glass calorimeter are insulated with cotton wool to:

options.text: minimize the exchange of heat with the surrounding air

blocks.explanation: Cotton wool insulation minimizes heat exchange with the surrounding air (6.6.1).

book_ref.quote: The outside walls of the calorimeter (beaker) are insulated using cotton wool

blocks.prompt: 48 The loose-fitting lid of a glass calorimeter keeps the contents at atmospheric pressure, so the heat measured equals:
blocks.explanation: Since the pressure inside is constant, the temperature measurement gives the enthalpy change ΔH (6.6.1).

book_ref.quote: a loose-fitting lid to keep the contents at atmospheric pressure

blocks.prompt: 49 In glass-calorimeter calculations the specific heat capacity of water is used for the solution because:

options.text: the solutions are so dilute that almost all their mass is water
the solute has a higher specific heat

blocks.explanation: Dilute solutions are almost all water by mass, so c of water is used (6.6.1).

book_ref.quote: The solutions we are using here are so dilute that almost all of their mass consists of water

blocks.prompt: 50 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH and the temperature rises by 6.8 K. Taking the mass as 100 g and c = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔH°n is:

book_ref.quote: Neutralization of 100 cm³ of 0.5 moldm⁻³ NaOH at 25°C

blocks.prompt: 51 How many moles of water are formed when 200 cm³ of 0.25 mol dm⁻³ HCl reacts completely with excess NaOH?
blocks.explanation: n = concentration × volume (dm³) = 0.25 × 0.200 = 0.050 mol HCl, giving 0.050 mol H₂O (6.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Calculation of n (no. of moles of H₂O formed): Using mole = Concentration(mol/dm³) x Volume (dm³)

blocks.text: 6.7 Enthalpy change and calorie content of food

blocks.prompt: 52 The energy released when food is digested in the body is:

options.text: always more than when burned outside
less than half of that when burned outside
the same as when it is burned outside the body

blocks.explanation: Digestion releases the same energy as burning outside the body, so ΔH of combustion gives the calorie content (6.7).

book_ref.quote: digestion of food releases same amount of energy as it is burned outside the body

blocks.prompt: 53 The heat of combustion of a food is typically determined in a:
blocks.explanation: The overall enthalpy of combustion of food is typically determined in a bomb calorimeter (6.7).

book_ref.quote: which can be determined in a calorimeter (typically in a bomb calorimeter)

blocks.prompt: 54 The calorie content of food is typically expressed in:
blocks.explanation: Calorie content is expressed in kilocalories (kcal) or joules (J) (6.7).

book_ref.quote: This energy is typically expressed in units of kilocalories (k cal) or joules (J).

blocks.prompt: 55 Glucose burns with ΔH° = –2803 kJ mol⁻¹ (molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹). How much energy is released by 45 g of glucose?

book_ref.quote: Molar mass of glucose is 180gmol⁻¹. Above equation shows that;

blocks.prompt: 56 Ethanol has ΔH°c = –1368 kJ mol⁻¹ and molar mass 46 g mol⁻¹. Using 4.184 kJ = 1 kcal, its calorie content is about:
blocks.explanation: ΔH per gram = 1368/46 = 29.74 kJ/g; calorie content = 29.74/4.184 = 7.11 kcal/g (6.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The enthalpy of combustion of a food (ΔHc) is the calorie content of that food

blocks.prompt: 57 The calorie content of glucose (ΔH° = –2803 kJ mol⁻¹, 180 g mol⁻¹) works out to:
blocks.explanation: ΔH = –2803/180 = –15.57 kJ/g; calorie content = –(–15.57)/4.184 = +3.72 kcal/g (book correction: the value is positive) (6.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The calorie content of glucose can be calculated as follows: First, we find ΔH per gram of glucose.

blocks.prompt: 58 The first law of thermodynamics is a manifestation of the law of:
blocks.explanation: The first law is the law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed (6.8).

book_ref.quote: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, but can be converted from one form to another.

blocks.prompt: 59 Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change in a chemical reaction is:

options.text: dependent on the number of steps
independent of the route, if initial and final conditions are the same

blocks.explanation: Hess's law: ΔH is independent of the route as long as the initial and final conditions are the same (6.8).

book_ref.quote: The total enthalpy change in a chemical reaction is independent of the route

blocks.prompt: 60 Hess's law is needed to find ΔH°f of CCl₄ because:

options.text: CCl₄ cannot be prepared directly by combining carbon and chlorine

blocks.explanation: ΔH cannot be measured directly when the compound cannot be made directly from its elements, e.g. CCl₄ (6.8).

book_ref.quote: tetrachloromethane CCl₄ cannot be prepared directly by combining carbon and chlorine

blocks.prompt: 61 In a Hess cycle, A → B directly, or A → M → N → B in steps. M and N are called:
blocks.explanation: Products formed along the indirect routes are reaction intermediates (6.8).

book_ref.quote: The products formed in these routes (M, N and X, Y, Z) are called reaction intermediates.

blocks.prompt: 62 For a direct route A → B (ΔHr) and an indirect route with steps ΔH₃, ΔH₄ and ΔH₅, Hess's law gives:
blocks.explanation: The sum of the step enthalpy changes equals ΔHr of the direct route (6.8).

book_ref.quote: Then according to Hess’ law,

blocks.prompt: 63 ΔH°f of CO₂ is –393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH°f of CO is –110.5 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH for CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g) is:

book_ref.quote: Calculate the enthalpy change of formation of CO using Hess cycle

blocks.prompt: 64 Given ΔH°f(C₂H₄) = +52.2 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH°f(C₂H₆) = –84.7 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH°r for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g) is:
blocks.explanation: ΔH°r = ΣΔH°f(products) – ΣΔH°f(reactants) = –84.7 – (52.2 + 0) = –136.9 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH°f(H₂) = 0 (6.8).

book_ref.quote: Calculate the enthalpy change of reaction of C₂H₄ + HCl → C₂H₅Cl

blocks.prompt: 65 In a Hess's law sum for ΔH°f of a fuel, the term for O₂(g) is taken as zero because:

options.text: O₂ does not take part in combustion
O₂ has the highest bond energy
O₂ is an element in its standard state, so its ΔH°f is zero

blocks.explanation: Book correction: it is the enthalpy of formation of O₂(g) that is zero, because O₂ is an element in its standard state (6.8).

book_ref.quote: Taking the heat of combustion of O₂(g) to be zero

blocks.prompt: 66 When 4.00 g of methane (16.0 g mol⁻¹) burns completely, 222.6 kJ of heat is evolved. The enthalpy of combustion of methane is:

book_ref.quote: The first step is to find the enthalpy change when one mole of propane is burned.

blocks.prompt: 67 Bond energies are used to estimate heats of reaction for:
blocks.explanation: The bond-energy method is a special case of Hess's law for gas-phase reactions (6.8).

book_ref.quote: A special case of Hess’ law involves the use of bond energies to estimate heats of reaction for gas-phase reactions.

blocks.prompt: 68 In the bond-energy method, the bond enthalpies of the product molecules are taken with a minus sign because:

options.text: the bonds are being formed instead of broken

blocks.explanation: In the second step product bonds are formed, so their bond enthalpies are taken with a minus sign: ΔH°rxn = ΣnER – ΣnEP (6.8).

book_ref.quote: which must now be taken with minus sign because the bonds are being formed instead of broken

blocks.prompt: 69 Using EH–H = 436, EBr–Br = 192 and EH–Br = 366 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 6.1), ΔH for H₂(g) + Br₂(g) → 2HBr(g) is:

book_ref.quote: In the case of formation of HCl(g) from H₂(g) and Cl₂(g)

blocks.prompt: 70 Using EN≡N = 945, EH–H = 436 and EN–H = 391 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 6.1), ΔH for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) is:

book_ref.quote: In the second step, the product molecules are formed.

blocks.prompt: 71 Using EC=C = 615, EH–H = 436, EC–C = 348 and EC–H = 413 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 6.1), ΔH for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g) is:
blocks.explanation: Only the changed bonds count: broken C=C + H–H = 615 + 436 = 1051 kJ; formed C–C + 2 C–H = 348 + 826 = 1174 kJ; ΔH = 1051 – 1174 = –123 kJ (6.8).

book_ref.quote: In the first step, the bonds in all the reactant molecules are broken to give free atoms in the gas phase.

blocks.prompt: 72 Using EH–H = 436, EF–F = 159 and EH–F = 563 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 6.1), the enthalpy of formation of HF(g) is about:

book_ref.quote: We replace this reaction by a hypothetical two-step process.

blocks.prompt: 73 The process of dissolving a solute in a solvent is called:
blocks.explanation: Dissolution is the process of dissolving a solute in a solvent (6.9).

book_ref.quote: The process of dissolving a solute in a solvent is called dissolution.

blocks.prompt: 74 Which is NOT one of the three assumed steps in the formation of a solution?

options.text: Burning the solute in excess oxygen

blocks.explanation: The three steps are expanding the solvent, breaking up the solute, and solute–solvent interaction (6.9).

book_ref.quote: Overcoming the intermolecular forces in the solvent to make room for the solute (expanding the solvent).

blocks.prompt: 75 The standard enthalpy of solution is the heat absorbed or evolved when one mole of a substance dissolves to give:
blocks.explanation: ΔH°sol is for one mole dissolved to give an infinitely dilute solution (6.9).

book_ref.quote: when one mole of a substance is dissolved in a solvent to give an infinitely dilute solution

blocks.prompt: 76 Which substance has an exothermic standard enthalpy of solution according to the chapter?
blocks.explanation: ΔH°sol of Na₂CO₃ = –25 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic); NH₄Cl, KCl and NH₄NO₃ are positive (6.9).

book_ref.quote: It is denoted by ΔH°sol and it may be exothermic or endothermic.

blocks.prompt: 77 According to Table 6.2, which ionic solid has the largest heat of solution?
blocks.explanation: Table 6.2: NaCl 4.98, KCl 17.8, KBr 19.9, KI 21.4, NH₄Cl 16.2, NH₄NO₃ 26.0 kJ mol⁻¹ (6.9).

book_ref.quote: Table 6.2 Heats of solution of some important ionic solids (kJ mol⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 78 The two factors that govern the dissolution of an ionic compound are:

options.text: electron affinity and ionization energy only

blocks.explanation: Hydration energy (attraction of ions with water) and lattice energy (breaking the ionic compound) govern dissolution (6.9).

book_ref.quote: Two factors govern the process of dissolution

blocks.prompt: 79 The process in which water molecules surround and interact with solute ions is called:
blocks.explanation: Hydration: water molecules surround and interact with solute ions (6.9.1).

book_ref.quote: The process in which water molecules surround and interact with the solute ions is called hydration.

blocks.prompt: 80 The forces between water molecules and ions in an aqueous solution are called:
blocks.explanation: Water molecules and ions are held by ion-dipole forces, so ions in aqueous solution are hydrated (6.9.1).

book_ref.quote: The forces are created between water molecules and the ions which are called ion-dipole forces

blocks.prompt: 81 The enthalpy of hydration of gaseous ions is:
